title: Advance Athlete Lab General Fitness and Strength Playbook
license: Owned content — cleared for AI retrieval

chunks.heading: FITT-VP as the prescription skeleton
chunks.body: Every session should specify Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type, Volume, and Progression. A complete strength prescription therefore reads: 3 days per week, 6-8 reps at roughly RPE 7, 45 min, full-body compound lifts, 3 sets per main lift, adding one set or a small load increase every one to two weeks. Missing any element makes the plan unauditable — the athlete cannot tell whether they did the session as intended, and progression becomes guesswork.

chunks.heading: Progressive overload without spikes
chunks.body: Progress one variable at a time: load, sets, reps, range of motion, or tempo. For beginners, add reps within a range before adding load, then reset reps at the higher load. Typical safe progression is 2.5-5% load on upper-body lifts and 5-10% on lower-body lifts, at most once a week per lift. Deload every fourth to sixth week by cutting volume roughly a third while keeping intensity. Never progress load and volume in the same week for the same lift.

chunks.heading: RPE and autoregulation
chunks.body: Rate of perceived exertion on a 1-10 scale lets a plan survive real life. RPE 5-6 is comfortable, 7-8 is challenging with 2-3 reps or a few minutes left in reserve, 9-10 is near maximal. On days when sleep, stress, or HRV is poor, hold the prescribed RPE and let load or pace drop rather than forcing the number on paper. Autoregulated sessions produce similar adaptations with fewer missed weeks than rigid percentage-based plans, especially for athletes training under 6 hours a week.

chunks.heading: Strength frequency and weekly set volume
chunks.body: Aim for each major muscle group to be trained at least twice a week. Roughly 10-20 hard sets per muscle group per week is a productive range for hypertrophy; strength-focused athletes can progress on fewer sets at higher intensity. With only two sessions a week, use full-body compound sessions. With three or four, either full-body or an upper/lower split works. Keep at least 48 hours between heavy sessions for the same muscle group, and place lower-body strength away from key running sessions.

chunks.heading: Beginner and intermediate weekly templates
chunks.body: Beginner, 3 days: full-body A/B alternating — squat pattern, hinge pattern, push, pull, carry or core, 2-3 sets of 8-12 at RPE 6-7, plus 10 min easy cardio. Intermediate, 4 days: upper/lower split with one heavier day (4-6 reps) and one moderate day (8-12 reps) per half, accessory work for weak points. Hybrid endurance plus strength, 4-5 days: two strength sessions on the same days as easy or short runs, quality endurance sessions on separate days, one full rest day. Always include mobility work for the athlete's restricted areas rather than a generic list.

chunks.heading: Mobility, warm-up, and recovery practices
chunks.body: Warm up with 5-10 min of easy general movement, then dynamic mobility for the joints the session loads, then two ramp-up sets or a few strides. Static stretching before heavy or explosive work can blunt output briefly; keep it for after sessions or standalone mobility days. Recovery levers in order of evidence strength: sleep duration and regularity, total energy and protein intake, easy-day discipline, and only then modalities like massage or compression. Two to three short mobility sessions a week beat one long occasional session.

chunks.heading: Volume load, mechanical tension, and CNS fatigue
chunks.body: Strength sessions are judged by volume load (sets x reps x load), mechanical tension on the target lifts, and how close the athlete worked to failure (RPE). Motor unit recruitment rises as loads get heavy and as sets approach failure; that is neuromuscular strain, not just 'getting a pump'. Central nervous system fatigue shows up as poor bar speed, missed reps, and lingering heaviness the next day, especially after poor sleep or low HRV. On those days, keep the prescribed RPE and let load drop rather than chasing last week's numbers. Active back limitations mean avoiding loaded spinal flexion and high-fatigue hinge volume. Acute:chronic spikes in lifting volume raise tissue risk the same way endurance spikes do.

chunks.heading: Yoga and mobility as down-regulation
chunks.body: Yoga and mobility sessions are recovery tools, not missed intervals. The coaching goal is parasympathetic up-regulation: slower breathing, lower heart rate, and a nervous system that can stand down after hard training. Improved vagal tone is inferred from resting HR, HRV, and how settled the athlete feels — it is coaching language, not a diagnosis. Myofascial work and long-range stretching help restricted areas when placed after training or on easy days. Do not pile impact or heavy spinal loading the next morning if the athlete has an active back limitation. A mobility session sitting on top of a high acute:chronic load is still the right medicine if it replaces intensity rather than adding to it.

chunks.heading: Warm-up and cool-down basics
chunks.body: 5–12 minutes easy movement before quality or strength; cool-down with easy spin/jog and light mobility. Skipping warm-ups raises injury risk on cold starts. Cool-downs are for transition, not a second workout.

chunks.heading: Sleep as a training pillar
chunks.body: Most adults need roughly 7+ hours; athletes often need more during heavy blocks. Poor sleep → soft-cap intensity. Protect wind-down, caffeine timing, and consistent schedules after travel.

chunks.heading: Hydration basics for training
chunks.body: Start sessions hydrated; in heat add fluids and sodium based on sweat. Overdrinking plain water in very long events can be harmful — individualize, and refer medical electrolyte disorders. Practice race hydration on long days.

chunks.heading: Daily steps and NEAT
chunks.body: Non-exercise activity helps health but endless steps on sore legs can impede recovery. On heavy training days, keep walks easy. Beginners: build steps before adding hard intervals.

chunks.heading: Full rest vs active recovery
chunks.body: Full rest: no structured training. Active recovery: very easy spin, walk, or mobility. Choose full rest when sleep is wrecked, illness threatens, or motivation is flattened with rising resting HR.

chunks.heading: Consistency beats perfection
chunks.body: Showing up four honest days beats one perfect week then burnout. Missed sessions happen — resume the next planned easy day without punishment doubles.

chunks.heading: Bodyweight strength options
chunks.body: Squat patterns, hinges (hip-dominant), pushes, pulls, and carries cover most needs. Tempo and range matter more than fancy machines. Progress reps before load when new.

chunks.heading: Desk-job athlete considerations
chunks.body: Long sitting stiffens hips and thoracic spine. Add mobility breaks and avoid only training after eight immobile hours without a warm-up. Evening quality may need longer warm-ups.

chunks.heading: Motivation is not readiness
chunks.body: Feeling fired up after coffee is not the same as recovered. Use sleep/HRV/resting HR. On red days, empathy then an easy session — do not confuse grit with good programming.

chunks.heading: Minimal effective dose
chunks.body: The smallest dose that moves the goal forward wins for busy athletes. Two quality-ish weeks of consistency beat sporadic hero weekends. Grow dose only when recovery keeps up.

chunks.heading: Protein — general coaching note
chunks.body: Spreading protein across meals supports recovery for many athletes. This is general coaching, not a clinical prescription or supplement stack. Refer disordered eating or kidney disease questions.

chunks.heading: Alcohol versus training quality
chunks.body: Alcohol impairs sleep and recovery signals. Heavy nights before quality or long days are poor tradeoffs. Empathy without lectures; direction to protect key sessions.

chunks.heading: Hotel-room fallback sessions
chunks.body: When gyms fail: bodyweight circuit, isometric holds, mobility flow, or easy stair walks. Keep RPE modest. Travel weeks are maintenance, not PR season.

chunks.heading: Accountability without shame
chunks.body: Check-ins ask what landed, not why the athlete is a failure. Missed days get a next action. Shame reduces honesty and increases injury concealment.
